title: Windblown lead carbonate as the main source of lead in blood of children from a seaside community: an example of local birds as "canaries in the mine".
ehr_evidence: Blood samples were collected from residents who wished to be tested, and analyzed for lead concentration and lead isotope ratios using thermal ionization mass spectrometry.
summary: Cross-sectional study evaluating blood lead levels and isotopic signatures in children and adults in Esperance, Western Australia, following a community exposure to windblown lead carbonate concentrate from a local port.
key_findings: Mean blood lead level in children was 7.5 µg/dL (range 1.5–25.7 µg/dL; n=49).
Magellan mine lead contributed 27% to 93% (mean 64%, median 71%) to children's blood lead.
A significant positive relationship was found between blood lead concentration and percentage of Magellan lead (R²=0.12, p=0.018).
Estimated background blood lead level for young children was approximately 2.3 µg/dL.
Inhalation of fine lead carbonate particles was identified as a significant exposure pathway for very young children and some adults.
captured_features: percentage contribution from Magellan mine lead
study_design: cross-sectional observational study with opportunistic blood sampling and isotopic source apportionment
data_source_type: primary biospecimen collection (blood) and environmental sampling
population: 49 children (mostly <5 years), 18 adults (>20 years), and 2 cord blood samples from Esperance, Western Australia
exposure_domain: environmental lead exposure from windblown lead carbonate concentrate at a shipping port
limitations: lack of isotopic data for environmental samples from individual houses
opportunistic sampling biased toward higher blood lead levels
small sample size for some subgroups
inability to fully identify non-Magellan lead sources
